title: The Wesleyan Chapel: Seneca Falls, July 1848
subtitle: The first woman's rights convention, Seneca Falls, New York, 19–20 July 1848, with London 1840, Rochester 1848 and Worcester 1850
intro: In June 1840 the World Anti-Slavery Convention met in London, and the American women sent as delegates were not allowed to take their seats. Lucretia Mott, a Philadelphia Quaker minister, recorded the exclusion in her travel diary in plain Quaker dating. Elizabeth Cady Stanton, a 24-year-old bride on her honeymoon, sat beside her as a spectator. Forty years later Stanton named that week as the beginning of the women's rights movement.

Eight years later, on 9 July 1848, five women met for tea at Jane Hunt's house outside Waterloo, New York, and decided to call a convention. They gave the public less than ten days' notice. On 16 July they drafted a Declaration of Sentiments at the M'Clintock family's parlour table, modelling it on the Declaration of Independence. On 19 and 20 July some three hundred people came to the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls. The Declaration was adopted unanimously. A resolution claiming the vote was contested, and later accounts say Frederick Douglass spoke to carry it. One hundred people signed: 68 women, and 32 men listed as 'present in favor of the movement'.

This room has an official record. The printed Report is the organisers' own minutes, and it is laid here beside dated letters, Douglass's editorial, the newspapers that reprinted and mocked the Declaration, and the minutes of the adjourned meeting at Rochester on 2 August, where Abigail Bush became one of the first women to preside over a mixed public meeting. The record is mostly letters, printed proceedings and newspapers rather than diaries. Much of the best-known detail comes from memoirs written decades later: Stanton's History of Woman Suffrage (1881) and Eighty Years and More (1898), and the recollections of the signers Charlotte Woodward and Rhoda Palmer. Those entries are marked as later accounts.

The press is reported here as it wrote. The Tribune printed the news straight, the Herald reprinted the Declaration, and upstate and Philadelphia papers ridiculed it. Stanton later wrote that many signers withdrew their names. The chapter ends at Worcester in October 1850, where the first national women's rights convention drew delegates from eleven states. Mott and Douglass were in the hall, and Stanton sent a letter.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Lucretia Mott's 1840 diary uses Quaker plain dating (for example '6th day, 6 mo. 12th' for Friday 12 June); these are converted here. Where the call's first printing is dated differently by different sources (11 or 14 July 1848), both are given.

eyes.name: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
eyes.role: Aged 24 on her London honeymoon in 1840; by 1848 aged 32, mother of three small sons, living in Seneca Falls
eyes.side: Reform circle of western New York; not a Quaker
eyes.where: Seneca Falls, New York; London in June 1840
eyes.form: dated letters, newspaper reply (1848); history written later (1881); memoir written later (1898)
eyes.authenticity: Her 1848 letters survive in manuscript and are edited in The Selected Papers of Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony, vol. 1 (Ann D. Gordon, ed., 1997). Her best-known accounts of London 1840 and of the convention come from History of Woman Suffrage vol. 1 (1881, co-edited with Anthony and Gage) and Eighty Years and More (1898), both written decades later and shaped by her later role as the movement's historian; where they are the only source, entries are marked approx.
eyes.bio: Daughter of a New York judge and wife of the abolitionist orator Henry B. Stanton, she met Lucretia Mott in London in 1840 when the women delegates were refused seats. Eight years later, restless in a small mill town, she pressed for a convention, drafted most of the Declaration of Sentiments and insisted on the resolution claiming the vote. Her angle is the organiser's: she wrote the text, defended it in print, and later wrote the story.

sources.title: Eighty Years and More (1898), Project Gutenberg
Eighty Years and More, ch. IX 'The First Woman's Rights Convention' (A Celebration of Women Writers)

eyes.name: Lucretia Coffin Mott
eyes.role: Hicksite Quaker minister from Philadelphia, aged 47 in 1840 and 55 in 1848; an official delegate of the Pennsylvania anti-slavery society in London
eyes.where: London, June 1840; visiting her sister in Auburn and friends in Waterloo, July 1848

waypoints.label: Auburn, staying with Martha Wright, July 1848

eyes.vantage_label: the famous speaker the town came to hear
eyes.authenticity: Her 1840 travel diary was published only in 1952, edited by Frederick B. Tolles as Slavery and 'The Woman Question' (Supplement 23 to the Journal of the Friends' Historical Society); it uses Quaker dating ('6th day, 6 mo. 12th'). Her letters are edited in Beverly Wilson Palmer, Selected Letters of Lucretia Mott (2002). Because the diary was first printed after 1928, it is not quoted here.
eyes.bio: The best-known woman speaker in American reform, she arrived in London as an elected delegate and was seated behind the bar as a spectator. In 1848 she was the draw that filled the Wesleyan Chapel, spoke at every session, and offered the closing resolution. She was cautious about the vote and about a woman presiding, and said so.

sources.title: Slavery and 'The Woman Question': Lucretia Mott's Diary, ed. F. B. Tolles (1952)
Tolles edition, bibliographic note (Worcester Women's History Project)

eyes.name: James Mott
eyes.role: Philadelphia wool merchant and Quaker, Lucretia's husband; chair of the second day at Seneca Falls
eyes.where: London 1840; the chair of the Wesleyan Chapel, 20 July 1848
eyes.form: published travel journal (1841); recorded in the printed Report
eyes.authenticity: His account of the 1840 voyage and convention was printed as Three Months in Great Britain (Philadelphia, 1841); its detail on the women's exclusion is summarised here only in general terms (approx). His role in 1848 is fixed by the printed Report.
eyes.bio: Quiet and supportive, he travelled with his wife to London and watched her excluded. In 1848 he was ill on the first day, then took the chair on the second, because the organisers did not yet think a woman should preside over a mixed meeting.

sources.title: Report of the Woman's Rights Convention (NPS transcription)

eyes.name: Frederick Douglass
eyes.role: Self-emancipated abolitionist, about 30, editor of The North Star in Rochester since December 1847
eyes.side: Abolitionists; the only African American known to have attended
eyes.vantage_label: editor and speaker in the room
eyes.form: dated letter; newspaper editorial; recorded in proceedings
eyes.authenticity: His letter of 14 July 1848 to Elizabeth M'Clintock survives and is published by the National Park Service; his editorial 'The Rights of Women' appeared in The North Star on 28 July 1848 (Library of Congress holds the issue). That he spoke for the franchise resolution in the afternoon of 20 July rests on later accounts by Stanton and others; the Report itself records his speeches in the morning discussion and the evening.
eyes.bio: Douglass printed the convention's call, travelled down to Seneca Falls, and was the man most associated afterwards with the vote resolution. The Report was printed at his newspaper's office, and his editorial was the first friendly notice in the press. His masthead already carried the line that right is of no sex.

sources.title: 'The Rights of Women', The North Star, 28 July 1848 (Library of Congress)
Text of the editorial (BlackPast)

eyes.name: Report of the Woman's Rights Convention (the printed Proceedings)
eyes.role: Official record compiled by a committee of five: M. A. M'Clintock, E. N. Foote, Amy Post, E. W. M'Clintock and E. C. Stanton
eyes.where: Wesleyan Chapel, Seneca Falls; printed by John Dick at the North Star office, Rochester
eyes.authenticity: A 12-page pamphlet printed in Rochester in 1848; the Library of Congress copy (NAWSA Collection) carries a title-page note by the attendee Rhoda Palmer. It is the organisers' own record and gives no hostile speech; it lists the 32 men separately as 'present in favor of the movement'. It does not single out the ninth resolution by name in its account of the voting.
eyes.bio: The Report is the room's own voice: sessions, hours, speakers and resolutions, the Declaration, and the hundred names. Its silences matter too: it does not name opponents, and it says only that some resolutions passed after debate by a large majority.

sources.title: NPS transcription of the Report
Library of Congress copy (rbcmiller001106)

eyes.name: Elizabeth W. M'Clintock (later Phillips)
eyes.role: About 27, unmarried daughter of the Waterloo druggist Thomas M'Clintock and Mary Ann M'Clintock
eyes.where: The M'Clintock house, Waterloo; the Wesleyan Chapel
eyes.vantage_label: the daughter of the drafting house
eyes.form: dated letters (received and written); recorded in the Report
eyes.authenticity: Letters to her from Stanton (14 July 1848) and Douglass (14 July 1848) survive and are quoted by the National Park Service (Women's Rights National Historical Park). Few of her own letters from 1848 are published; her part is chiefly fixed by the Report and by Stanton's statement that the two of them wrote replies to the newspapers.
eyes.bio: She invited Douglass, helped draft at her parents' parlour table, spoke on the first afternoon and sat on the committee that published the Report. A year later she tried to enter business and was turned away as too old and inexperienced; she later ran her own shop in Philadelphia.

sources.title: NPS: Elizabeth M'Clintock

eyes.name: Martha Coffin Wright
eyes.role: Lucretia Mott's younger sister, 42, of Auburn, New York; several months pregnant in July 1848
eyes.where: Auburn; the Hunt tea in Waterloo; the Wesleyan Chapel
eyes.authenticity: Her letters are in the Garrison Family Papers, Sophia Smith Collection, Smith College. Her humorous newspaper piece read at the convention is recorded in the Report; its title and the newspaper are not identified there.
eyes.bio: One of the five at the Hunt tea, she brought a satirical pen and the household view of a mother of a large family. She went on to preside over national conventions in the 1850s and 1860.

sources.title: NPS: Martha C. Wright

eyes.name: Charlotte Woodward (later Pierce)
eyes.role: Aged 18, a farm girl who sewed gloves at home for local makers
eyes.side: Working young women of Seneca County
eyes.where: Came by wagon from near Waterloo; signed the Declaration
eyes.form: memoir (written later): recollections given in 1916 and 1920
eyes.authenticity: Her memories were set down seventy years later: an interview in the Philadelphia Evening Public Ledger (1916) and Rheta Childe Dorr's piece 'The Eternal Question' in Collier's (30 October 1920), which Dorr assembled from piecemeal conversations. A later paraphrase (Katzenstein, 1955) differs on details. Whether she ever voted is disputed.
eyes.bio: She is the voice of the ordinary attender: a young pieceworker who came because she wanted her own earnings. As the last surviving signer in 1920, she became the bridge between Seneca Falls and the Nineteenth Amendment.

sources.title: 100 Signers Project: Charlotte Woodward

eyes.name: Rhoda J. Palmer
eyes.role: About 32, a Waterloo-area woman who came with her father
eyes.where: In the Wesleyan Chapel; a signer
eyes.form: memoir (written later); annotation on her copy of the Report
eyes.authenticity: Her short reminiscence survives in the Miller NAWSA Suffrage Scrapbooks (1897–1911) at the Library of Congress, and her manuscript note is written on the title page of the Library's copy of the Report. The year of writing is not established here.
eyes.bio: Palmer offers the pew-level view: who could speak, who came with whom, and a closing note of patience. She lived long enough to see New York women win the state vote in 1917.

sources.title: Rhoda J Palmer's memories (Library of Congress item, via SCU exhibit)
Library of Congress copy of the Report with her note

eyes.name: Minutes of the Rochester Woman's Rights Convention (secretaries)
eyes.role: Manuscript minutes kept by the secretaries Catharine A. F. Stebbins, Sarah L. Hallowell and Mary H. Hallowell
eyes.authenticity: The manuscript minutes are held at the University of Rochester (Rare Books, Special Collections) and transcribed in its Scripto project, with illegible passages and editorial insertions. A 1948 study in Rochester History supplies further detail from the printed proceedings and local press.
eyes.bio: The minutes show the meeting the Seneca Falls organisers adjourned to: Amy Post opening it, a woman elected to preside, and Lucretia Mott arguing with a friendly speaker over flattery.

sources.title: University of Rochester Scripto transcription, first page
Rochester History vol. 10 (1948)

eyes.name: Abigail Norton Bush
eyes.role: Rochester abolitionist, about 38; elected president of the Rochester convention
eyes.where: The chair of the Unitarian Church, Rochester
eyes.vantage_label: the first woman in the chair
eyes.form: memoir (written later): letter of 1898 to Susan B. Anthony
eyes.authenticity: Her recollection is a letter to Anthony written fifty years afterwards (University of Rochester); contemporary detail of her presiding comes from the Rochester minutes and press.
eyes.bio: Elected over the objections of Mott and Stanton, who feared a woman in the chair would discredit the meeting, she presided calmly; half a century later she reflected that it had ended the belief that women needed a man to preside.

sources.title: University of Rochester exhibit: Seneca Falls and Rochester conventions

eyes.name: The newspapers (Courier, Tribune, Herald, Oneida Whig, Mechanic's Advocate, Public Ledger)
eyes.role: Editors and correspondents, friendly and hostile
eyes.where: Seneca Falls, New York City, Utica, Albany, Philadelphia
eyes.authenticity: The Tribune (29 July) and Herald (30 July) items are on Chronicling America. The hostile lines from the Oneida Whig, Mechanic's Advocate and Public Ledger are known chiefly as Stanton and Anthony reprinted them in History of Woman Suffrage vol. 1 (1881); their exact issue dates are not verified here.
eyes.bio: The papers were the convention's largest audience. Several printed the Declaration nearly whole, some to praise it and more to mock it; the ridicule spread the text further than the organisers could have.

sources.title: Library of Congress: 1848 newspaper coverage
New York Herald, 30 July 1848, p. 3 (Chronicling America)

entries.headline: Mott meets a young bride named Elizabeth Stanton
entries.digest: Among the American abolitionists gathering in London, Mott noted meeting James G. Birney and Henry B. Stanton, with Stanton's young wife Elizabeth. It is the first recorded meeting of the two women. Nothing in the entry marks it as important.
entries.source_note: Tolles ed. (1952), p. 22, with editor's note that this was their first meeting.

entries.headline: A walk with the Stantons to Newgate Street
entries.digest: A plain social line: Mott walked with Henry and Elizabeth Stanton to Newgate Street. The acquaintance was already becoming a friendship before the convention opened.
entries.source_note: Tolles ed., p. 24.

entries.headline: British abolitionists ask the women to stand down
entries.digest: Joseph Sturge and others called on the American women delegates. A meeting of the women was arranged to draw up a protest against their expected exclusion.
entries.source_note: Tolles ed., p. 27.

entries.headline: A written protest, and pressure to stay away
entries.digest: The women's protest was drafted and signed by Sarah Pugh on their behalf. That evening several men urged them not to present their credentials at all; Mott recorded that one clergyman, Nathaniel Colver, was blunt and left angry.
entries.source_note: Tolles ed., pp. 28–29.

entries.place: Freemasons' Hall, Great Queen Street, London
entries.headline: The convention opens; the women are seated as spectators
entries.digest: The World Anti-Slavery Convention assembled. After Wendell Phillips moved to admit the women delegates and a long debate followed, the women were kept from membership and seated behind the bar. Mott recorded the courtesies and introductions as well as the exclusion.
entries.source_note: Tolles ed., pp. 29–31.

entries.headline: Arm in arm, a resolve to hold a women's convention
entries.digest: In the History of Woman Suffrage, written four decades later, Stanton placed the origin of Seneca Falls on the night the women were refused seats: she and Mott walked arm in arm down Great Queen Street and agreed to hold a convention for women's rights once home. No 1840 document records the resolution.
entries.source_note: History of Woman Suffrage vol. 1 (1881), excerpt at Digital History Reader (Virginia Tech) evidence 14; date as given in that later account.

entries.headline: A husband records his wife's exclusion
entries.digest: James Mott's published account of the journey, Three Months in Great Britain, described the convention and the debate over the women's credentials from the floor. He had come as a supporter, not a delegate's guardian, and his record of the vote is a man's view from inside the bar.
entries.source_note: Three Months in Great Britain (Philadelphia, 1841); page not checked.

entries.headline: Garrison arrives and refuses to take his seat
entries.digest: Mott noted the arrival of William Lloyd Garrison, Nathaniel Rogers, Charles Remond and William Adams. Garrison's party resolved not to enter a convention from which the women were excluded and sat in the gallery instead.
entries.source_note: Tolles ed., pp. 35–36.

entries.headline: Disappointment at women's lack of independent action
entries.digest: Mott wrote that she was much disappointed to see so little independent action among women. A meeting of delegates was called for the evening. The entry shows her frustration aimed as much at women's caution as at men's rules.
entries.source_note: Tolles ed., p. 38.

entries.headline: Tea at Jane Hunt's
entries.digest: Mott, visiting her sister Martha Wright at Auburn, came to Richard and Jane Hunt's house outside Waterloo. With Hunt, Wright, Mary Ann M'Clintock and Stanton, the only non-Quaker present, she agreed to call a convention within ten days.
entries.source_note: NPS, 'Jane Hunt' (Women's Rights NHP).

entries.headline: Stanton pours out her discontent
entries.digest: Stanton later wrote that she arrived at the Hunts' with a 'general discontent' built from isolation, housework and illness in Seneca Falls, and spoke so vehemently that the women decided to act at once. The call was written that evening.
entries.source_note: Eighty Years and More (1898), ch. IX; written fifty years later.

entries.headline: One of five at the tea table
entries.digest: Martha Wright came from Auburn with her sister and sat at the Hunt tea. She was several months pregnant and would carry that household knowledge into the satire she wrote for the convention.
entries.source_note: NPS, 'Jane Hunt' and 'Martha C. Wright'.

entries.headline: The call appears in the Seneca County Courier
entries.digest: An unsigned notice announced a convention at the Wesleyan Chapel on 19 and 20 July to discuss the social, civil and religious condition and rights of woman, with the first day reserved for women. The National Park Service dates its first appearance to 11 July; Stanton's own memoir gives 14 July.
entries.source_note: NPS 'Jane Hunt' (11 July); Eighty Years and More ch. IX and University of Rochester exhibit (14 July).

entries.headline: 'Rain or shine' to Waterloo on Sunday
entries.digest: On Friday morning Stanton wrote to Elizabeth M'Clintock that she would spend Sunday with the family whatever the weather, to prepare the convention's papers. The letter shows how little time was left: five days.
entries.source_note: Letter to E. W. M'Clintock, 14 July 1848, quoted by NPS 'Elizabeth M'Clintock'.

entries.headline: Douglass accepts an invitation
entries.digest: Writing from Rochester, Douglass told Elizabeth M'Clintock he would gladly accept her invitation and expected one or more of the Post family to come as well. The same day The North Star carried the convention's call.
entries.source_note: Douglass to E. W. M'Clintock, 14 July 1848, quoted by NPS 'Amy Post' and 'Elizabeth M'Clintock'.

entries.headline: James is unwell; Martha will come
entries.digest: Mott sent Stanton a note apologising that James was quite unwell and might miss the first day. She promised to bring Martha Wright, and that both sisters would be there for both days.
entries.source_note: Mott to Stanton, 16 July 1848, as summarised in secondary accounts; manuscript not seen.

entries.headline: Drafting in the M'Clintock parlour
entries.digest: At her parents' house the organisers met again to write the Declaration and resolutions. Elizabeth M'Clintock took part. The small mahogany table they used was later bought by Stanton and is now at the Smithsonian.
entries.source_note: NPS 'Elizabeth M'Clintock'; Smithsonian NMAH object 529599; Duke Library note on Stanton's 1897 letter.

entries.headline: Choosing the Declaration of 1776 as the model
entries.digest: Stanton's later account says the women looked through reports of other reform societies for a form, then read the Declaration of Independence aloud and adapted it, listing grievances against 'man' as 1776 had listed them against the King. She went home to revise the grievances and resolutions at her own desk.
entries.source_note: History of Woman Suffrage vol. 1 (1881); later account.

entries.headline: The vote clause divides the household
entries.digest: Stanton added a demand for the elective franchise. Mott warned it would make them ridiculous, and Henry Stanton, who was about to stand for office, objected and left town before the convention. These details come from later family and movement accounts.
entries.source_note: Later accounts (Stanton's reminiscences; Rochester History 1948, which notes her husband and friends advised against it).

entries.headline: Women only: the Declaration read paragraph by paragraph
entries.digest: The convention met with women only. Mary M'Clintock was named secretary, Stanton stated the purpose, and Mott urged women not to let novelty keep them silent. The Declaration was read, re-read clause by clause and amended. Whether to seek men's signatures was debated and put off to the next day.
entries.source_note: Report, Wednesday morning (NPS transcription).

entries.headline: With her father, in the pews
entries.digest: Rhoda Palmer remembered coming with her father and that only women spoke on the first day, though men were present. She closed her short memoir with a farmer's image of patience.
entries.quote: The seed fell on good ground, But the end is not yet.
entries.source_note: Rhoda J. Palmer's memories, Miller NAWSA Scrapbooks, Library of Congress; written later.

entries.headline: A wagon, then a procession
entries.digest: Charlotte Woodward recalled setting out by wagon with friends, sure no one else would come, and finding other wagons joining on the road. By the time they reached the chapel they were a procession. She had come because she sewed gloves secretly at home for a pittance she could not keep.
entries.source_note: Dorr, 'The Eternal Question', Collier's, 30 Oct 1920; via 100 Signers Project.

entries.headline: Her satire read aloud by her sister
entries.digest: In the afternoon session Lucretia Mott read a humorous newspaper article written by Martha C. Wright. The Report does not give the title, but it is the only piece of comedy entered in the official record.
entries.source_note: Report, Wednesday afternoon.

entries.headline: A daughter addresses the convention
entries.digest: After the resolutions were read, including the ninth on the franchise, Elizabeth W. M'Clintock gave an address and the meeting adjourned to ten the next morning.
entries.source_note: Report, Wednesday afternoon.

entries.headline: Mott on the progress of reforms
entries.digest: To a large mixed audience Mott spoke on reform in general. She was the convention's best-known speaker, and the evening drew the crowd.
entries.source_note: Report, Wednesday evening.

entries.headline: James Mott takes the chair
entries.digest: Recovered enough to attend, James Mott of Philadelphia presided. The organisers had chosen a man for the mixed sessions; Stanton re-read the Declaration and the floor opened to debate.
entries.source_note: Report, Thursday morning.

entries.headline: The Declaration adopted unanimously
entries.digest: Mott, Douglass, Amy Post and Thomas and Mary Ann M'Clintock spoke on the Declaration, which was then adopted unanimously. It opens by rewriting 1776, and lists among its grievances that woman had never been allowed the elective franchise.
entries.quote: all men and women are created equal
entries.source_note: Report, Thursday morning; Declaration text.

entries.headline: Resolutions taken one by one
entries.digest: The resolutions of the day before were taken up separately. Some passed with little comment; others, after much debate and slight alteration, passed by a large majority. The ninth resolved that women should secure their right to vote. Sixty-eight women signed the Declaration, and 32 men were listed as in favour.
entries.quote: their sacred right to the elective franchise
entries.source_note: Report, Thursday afternoon; ninth resolution; signature lists.

entries.headline: Douglass backs the vote
entries.digest: Later accounts place Douglass on his feet for the franchise resolution when it was in danger, arguing that women should have the same political rights as men. The Report records him in the morning debate and, in the evening, ably supporting the cause of woman.
entries.source_note: Report (morning and evening); afternoon role from later accounts incl. Rochester History (1948) and Woodward's recollection.

entries.headline: The last resolution: men and women together
entries.digest: Mott offered a final resolution: that success required the efforts of both men and women, to overthrow the pulpit's monopoly and open trades, professions and commerce to women. It passed. She closed the convention with an address of nearly an hour.
entries.quote: the speedy success of our cause depends upon the zealous
entries.source_note: Report, Thursday evening.

entries.headline: Stanton answers the usual charges
entries.digest: Stanton spoke in defence of women against the common accusations made by men, Thomas M'Clintock read Blackstone on a wife's legal status, and Stanton was named to the five-person committee to publish the proceedings.
entries.source_note: Report, Thursday evening.

entries.headline: An eighteen-year-old signs
entries.digest: Woodward signed among the 68 women. Seventy years later she remembered that only Stanton and Douglass had wholeheartedly backed the vote, and that some women signed as if it were a death warrant.
entries.source_note: Dorr, Collier's, 30 Oct 1920; recollection written much later.

entries.headline: 'The Rights of Women' in The North Star
entries.digest: Douglass called the convention one of the most interesting events of the week and described its participants as intelligent and dignified. He held woman entitled to every political right claimed for man and saw no reason to deny her the vote. He also observed that the rights of animals would be discussed with more complacency.
entries.source_note: The North Star, 28 July 1848, p. 3 (LOC); text at BlackPast.

entries.headline: The Tribune prints the news
entries.digest: The New-York Daily Tribune ran 'Woman's Rights—A Convention' with the Declaration, in a straight report. Horace Greeley's paper would later take the claim more seriously than most.
entries.source_note: New-York Daily Tribune, 29 July 1848, p. 2 (Chronicling America, via LOC blog).

entries.headline: The Herald reprints the Declaration
entries.digest: James Gordon Bennett's New York Herald printed most of the Declaration on page three. Reprinting, whether to inform or to amuse, carried the text across the country.
entries.source_note: New York Herald, 30 July 1848, p. 3 (Chronicling America).

entries.headline: The Oneida Whig: 'shocking and unnatural'
entries.digest: The Whig called the convention the most shocking and unnatural incident in the history of 'womanity' and asked who would cook if ladies voted and legislated.
entries.quote: where, gentlemen, will be our dinners and our elbows?
entries.source_note: As reprinted in History of Woman Suffrage vol. 1 (1881); issue date not verified.

entries.headline: The Mechanic's Advocate: unwomanly
entries.digest: The Albany paper argued that every true-hearted woman would find the demands unwomanly, and that success would degrade women from their sphere and injure everyone.
entries.quote: a monstrous injury to all mankind
entries.source_note: As reprinted in History of Woman Suffrage vol. 1; issue date not verified.

entries.headline: The two conventions 'greatly encouraging'
entries.digest: Back home, Mott wrote that the summer's two conventions were greatly encouraging and gave hope that a long-neglected subject would at last get attention.
entries.source_note: Letter of August 1848, cited in secondary accounts; recipient and exact date not verified.

entries.headline: Amy Post opens; a woman is elected to preside
entries.digest: The adjourned convention was opened by Amy Post. Abigail Bush was elected president, Laura Murray vice-president. William C. Nell read an address; Mott objected to calling women the better half of creation, saying men flattered women without thinking. A letter from Gerrit Smith was read, and the Seneca Falls Declaration was put to discussion, with Stanton speaking.
entries.source_note: Rochester minutes, first page (University of Rochester Scripto).

entries.headline: Presiding over a mixed meeting
entries.digest: Bush took the chair although Mott and Stanton feared a woman presiding would discredit the cause. Contemporary reports had her running the sessions calmly. In 1898 she told Anthony it had ended the idea that women's meetings needed a man in the chair.
entries.source_note: Rochester History (1948); University of Rochester exhibit citing Bush to Anthony, 1898.

entries.headline: Mott: some resolutions 'much too tame'
entries.digest: At Rochester Mott rebuked a young Yale-trained man who said women should not interpret Scripture, and thought several resolutions too tame. The meeting resolved to petition every year until the prayer was granted.
entries.source_note: Rochester History vol. 10 (1948).

entries.headline: Douglass speaks again
entries.digest: On home ground Douglass spoke for the emancipation of women, with William C. Bloss of Rochester adding similar views laced with jokes about women voting.
entries.source_note: Rochester History vol. 10 (1948).

entries.headline: Signers withdraw their names
entries.digest: Stanton recalled that the press, pulpit and parlour turned on them, and that many women who had signed withdrew their names and joined the critics. She thought the ridicule was nonetheless useful, since it spread the ideas.
entries.quote: All the journals from Maine to Texas seemed to strive
entries.source_note: Eighty Years and More (1898), ch. IX; names and numbers of withdrawals not given.

entries.headline: Stanton answers the National Reformer
entries.digest: Stanton replied in print to charges by George G. Cooper, editor of the Rochester National Reformer, for readers who did not yet understand the real objects of the conventions at Rochester and Seneca Falls. Her later memoir says she and Elizabeth M'Clintock wrote such replies together.
entries.source_note: National Reformer, 14 Sept 1848 (LOC scrapbook via LOC blog); Rochester History (1948).

entries.headline: Turned away from a silk business
entries.digest: Elizabeth M'Clintock asked the silk merchant Edward Davis to take her on as an apprentice; he declined, saying she was too old and inexperienced. The 1850 census listed her as a clerk in her father's drugstore, the only Waterloo woman with an occupation recorded.
entries.source_note: NPS 'Elizabeth M'Clintock'.

entries.headline: The first national convention
entries.digest: At Worcester, with Paulina Wright Davis elected president, Mott spoke at length on women's condition and the convention's duties. Wendell Phillips's resolution that parties should write equality before the law without distinction of sex or color on their banners came before the evening session.
entries.source_note: Proceedings of the 1850 National Women's Rights Convention (WWHP edition).

entries.headline: A letter read in her place
entries.digest: Stanton did not come to Worcester; her letter was read to the morning session by M. A. W. Johnson. The movement she had started in a village chapel now met with delegates from eleven states.
entries.source_note: Proceedings (WWHP); Mass Moments.

entries.headline: On the Business Committee
entries.digest: Douglass sat on the Business Committee and spoke in the afternoon discussion, the same session at which Sojourner Truth spoke.
entries.source_note: Proceedings (WWHP).

entries.headline: Stanton asks to buy the table
entries.digest: Nearly fifty years on, Stanton wrote to Sarah M'Clintock asking whether she would sell the table on which the Declaration had been written, and for what price. The purchase went through, and the table became a relic of the movement.
entries.source_note: Duke University Libraries, letter to Sarah M'Clintock dated 31 March [1897].

entries.headline: The last signer, in Collier's
entries.digest: In Collier's, Rheta Childe Dorr presented Woodward as the only living signer of 1848, weeks before the first presidential election under the Nineteenth Amendment. Her story of secret glove-making and the wagon procession became the standard picture of the ordinary signer.
entries.source_note: Dorr, 'The Eternal Question', Collier's, 30 Oct 1920 (100 Signers Project).

claims.claim: First National Woman's Rights Convention at Worcester elects Paulina Wright Davis president

convergences.label: Women delegates refused seats in London
convergences.note: Mott's same-day diary records courtesy and exclusion in a matter-of-fact tone; Stanton's account forty years later turns the evening into the origin of a movement; James Mott wrote it up for American readers.

convergences.label: Tea at Jane Hunt's in Waterloo
convergences.note: The Park Service record fixes the day; Stanton's memoir makes it her outburst of discontent; Wright, pregnant and a guest, would turn that discontent into comedy.

convergences.label: Five days' notice: letters fly to the M'Clintocks
convergences.note: Stanton and Douglass both wrote to Elizabeth M'Clintock that Friday, and the call ran in The North Star; the small Quaker network did the organising.

convergences.label: Drafting at the M'Clintock table
convergences.note: Mott writes of illness and logistics; the M'Clintock daughter's home becomes the workshop; Stanton's later account gives the moment its 1776 template.

convergences.label: First day: women only, men listening
convergences.note: The Report records order and amendment; Palmer and Woodward, writing decades later, remember the road and the pews; Wright's satire is the one joke in the minutes.

convergences.label: Second day: Declaration, resolutions, signatures
convergences.note: The official record says 'large majority' without naming the ninth; the later accounts make the vote resolution the drama and Douglass its rescuer.

convergences.label: The first week of press
convergences.note: Douglass's North Star argued the principle within eight days; the Tribune and Herald reprinted the Declaration; upstate and Philadelphia papers answered with ridicule.

convergences.label: The adjourned convention at Rochester
convergences.note: The minutes show Mott quarrelling with a friendly speaker about flattery; Bush takes the chair Mott and Stanton thought premature.

convergences.label: Worcester: the national convention
convergences.note: Mott and Douglass are in the hall; Stanton is a letter read aloud; the scale has grown from a village chapel to eleven states.

ties.note: First met in London on 5 June 1840, per Mott's diary; co-organisers in 1848.
Wife and husband; both in London in 1840 and at Seneca Falls in 1848, where he presided.
Sisters; Mott was staying with Wright in Auburn when the tea took place, and read Wright's satire to the convention.
She invited him; his acceptance of 14 July 1848 survives.
Stanton wrote to her on 14 July 1848, drafted at her family's table, and later said they co-wrote replies to the newspapers.
The Report was printed by John Dick at the North Star office in Rochester.
His editorial of 28 July answered the ridicule other papers were printing.
She replied to the National Reformer's charges in September 1848.
Mott and Stanton feared a woman presiding at Rochester; Bush presided.
Woodward remembered Stanton and Douglass as the vote resolution's only firm champions.
Palmer's manuscript note is written on the title page of the Library of Congress copy of the Report.
The minutes record her election as president on 2 August 1848.

threads_out.note: The Declaration of Sentiments rewrote 1776, but its demand ran into the settlement of 1787: the Constitution left the qualifications of voters to the states, so the women of 1848 aimed their franchise resolution at New York and the other states, and the long route to a federal amendment began there.

Douglass, who spoke for the vote at Seneca Falls, recruited Black soldiers during the war; Stanton and Susan B. Anthony suspended the women's conventions and in 1863 founded the Women's Loyal National League to petition for the abolition of slavery by constitutional amendment.

The 1840 London convention that excluded Mott was a gathering of the British anti-slavery movement whose earlier campaign had pressed the powers at Vienna to condemn the slave trade in 1815; Thomas Clarkson, a veteran of that campaign, opened the 1840 meeting.

Charlotte Woodward, the last surviving signer, lived to see the Nineteenth Amendment ratified in 1920; a year earlier the Inter-Allied Women's Conference, led by suffragists of the international alliance that Anthony had helped found, lobbied the peacemakers in Paris for women's rights.
